name: AP World History: Modern
overview: AP World History: Modern covers world history from c. 1200 CE to the present, organized around themes such as governance, economic systems, cultural developments, social structures, technology, and interactions with the environment. Students analyze primary and secondary sources and write arguments using historical thinking skills: causation, comparison, and continuity and change over time.
examMode: Fully digital in Bluebook (all answers, including essays, typed in the app)

sections.name: Section I, Part A
sections.notes: Sets of 3–4 questions, each set tied to a primary source, secondary source, chart, map, or image. Four answer choices (A–D).

sections.name: Section I, Part B
sections.notes: All three required (from May 2027). Q1 uses one or more secondary text sources, Q2 a primary text source, Q3 a primary or secondary non-text source (chart, map, image). Each question covers a different period between 1491 and 2001. Each is 3 points (parts a, b, c).

sections.name: Section II, Question 1
sections.notes: Seven documents. The 60 minutes include a 15-minute reading period. Scored on a 7-point rubric.

sections.name: Section II, Question 2
sections.notes: From May 2027: one required broad prompt with a brief introductory statement; you choose the evidence and line of reasoning. Scored on a 6-point rubric.

skills.name: Developments and Processes
skills.description: Identify and explain historical concepts, developments, and processes.

skills.name: Sourcing and Situation
skills.description: Identify and explain a source's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and audience, and why those matter.

skills.name: Claims and Evidence in Sources
skills.description: Identify and describe the claim or argument in a source and the evidence it uses; compare arguments of two sources.

skills.name: Contextualization
skills.description: Explain the broader historical context of a development or process.

skills.name: Making Connections
skills.description: Use the reasoning processes (comparison, causation, continuity and change) to explain relationships among developments.

skills.name: Argumentation
skills.description: Develop a defensible claim, support it with evidence, and explain how the evidence supports, corroborates, or qualifies the argument.

scoring.summary: Multiple choice (55 questions) is 40% of the composite; there is no penalty for wrong answers. The three SAQs (3 points each) are 20%, the DBQ (7 points) is 25%, and the LEQ (6 points) is 15%. College Board converts the weighted composite to a 1–5 score using cut points set each year through equating; the cut points are not published. Rubric points on the essays are each earned independently, so a weak thesis does not block evidence or contextualization points.

frqTypes.name: Short-answer question (SAQ)
frqTypes.howScored: Three parts (a, b, c), 1 point each, earned independently. Parts usually ask you to describe or explain one piece of evidence, a cause, an effect, or a difference between two interpretations. One accurate, specific, and relevant sentence or two per part is enough; no thesis is needed.

frqTypes.name: Document-based question (DBQ)
frqTypes.howScored: Thesis (1), contextualization (1), evidence from documents (2: describe 3 documents for 1 point, use 4 documents to support an argument for 2), evidence beyond the documents (1), sourcing — explain the relevance of point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience for 2 documents (1), and complex understanding (1).

frqTypes.name: Long essay question (LEQ)
frqTypes.howScored: Thesis (1), contextualization (1), evidence (2: identify two specific examples for 1, use two to support an argument for 2), analysis and reasoning (2: use comparison, causation, or continuity/change to frame the argument for 1; demonstrate a complex understanding for 2).

strategy: Multiple choice runs at about one minute per question. Read the source attribution (author, date, audience) before the excerpt; many questions are answered by knowing when and why the source was written.

For 'which of the following most directly caused/influenced' questions, eliminate answers that are true but from the wrong period. The best answer must come before the source and connect to it directly.
On SAQs, start each part with the task verb's answer in the first sentence, then add one sentence of specific evidence (a named law, event, person, or date). Label parts (a), (b), (c).
Use the DBQ's 15-minute reading period to sort documents into two or three argument groups and to jot one sourcing note (why this author, this audience, this moment) beside at least two documents.

Earn the DBQ evidence points deliberately: describe at least four documents in your own words and tie each to your claim, then add one specific outside example you clearly label as not from the documents.
Write the thesis as a claim plus reasons ('X happened largely because of A and B, although C limited it'). A thesis with a 'although' clause often sets up the complexity point.
Contextualization should describe developments before or around the prompt's time frame in three or four sentences, not a one-line 'throughout history' opener.

For the 2027-format LEQ, pick the evidence you know best within the prompt's time frame. Two well-explained specific examples earn full evidence credit; four tied to a nuanced argument can help earn complexity.
Budget time: about 13 minutes per SAQ, 45 minutes writing the DBQ after reading, and 40 minutes for the LEQ (including 5 minutes of planning).
pitfalls: Quoting documents instead of describing them; quotation alone does not earn evidence credit.
Sourcing by identifying ('the author is a senator') without explaining how that affects the document's meaning or reliability for your argument.
Choosing MCQ answers that are true facts but do not answer the specific question about the excerpt.
Confusing similar items across periods: the Ottoman vs. Mughal vs. Safavid empires, the Atlantic revolutions vs. later independence movements, and the two world wars' causes.
Writing contextualization that is only a sentence, or that drifts decades away from the prompt.
Running out of time on the LEQ because the DBQ ran long.
Treating Units 1, 2, and 9 as skippable; they appear in multiple choice and can anchor SAQs.

caveats: Klutch built this profile from the AP U.S. History exam research (both exams share the same section structure and rubrics) plus the World History unit list and weightings from the Course and Exam Description; recheck details against AP Central.
Approximate cutoffs are Klutch estimates; College Board does not publish cut scores.
